name: Jade Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government. We sell nothing or campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential, with no name attached. What does a normal shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the airline baggage-claims calls at a contact centre, mostly evening flights. A traveller's suitcase has gone to the wrong city, and I trace the tag through the flight record while another agent speaks to the airport desk. I have a two-year college diploma and am one of the best on missing-bag claims, especially when two flights have nearly the same number.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy there, and how does home fit around it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a bag back before someone has to buy clothes for an important meeting. I use the approved AI search daily but always check the baggage tag against the flight record. My partner David runs a small shoe-repair stall, our grown daughter rents her own flat, and my high evening rate helped us save roughly eleven months of expenses; I also sew straps on our old cases at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims desk that a quicker search is welcome if the flight number is still checked. A tidy answer cannot put a case on the correct carousel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The evening flights and missing bags will keep coming, so I expect my paid work to continue. Eleven months saved means David and I can handle an ordinary bad month without calling our daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep matching baggage tags to flight records and show the newer agents how the existing AI search misses a changed gate. In the first year of AI Plateau I would put three wrong-gate examples in the team handbook and keep the checking step on every delayed bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm; I know the work, and our money can take a small bump. I would still be cross if a customer went to the wrong airport because our note looked pretty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What detail changed that bag search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bag once showed as arrived because the flight number matched, but the date was a day old. The real tag scan had it waiting on a trolley in another city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: David can repair a shoe heel faster than I can, but neither of us needs to turn a small AI saving into a new purchase. We would keep our eleven months for an actual gap.

say: I would welcome **faster search** with a flight-date check.
I would tell agents **wrong gates** belong in the team handbook.
think: I expect my **evening claims work** to continue because flights and missing bags remain common.
I trust our **eleven-month reserve** for an ordinary gap.
do: Keep matching **bag tags** to flight records and coach new agents on changed gates.
Add **three wrong-gate cases** to the handbook while keeping the check on delayed bags.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages, though watchful of wrong locations.
S0.quote: A tidy answer cannot put a case on the correct carousel.
fieldNote: She uses **AI search daily** but verifies each tag against a dated flight record.
Her **eleven-month reserve** makes a minor software change financially manageable without drawing on her grown daughter.

steps.text: Keep checking baggage tags against dated flight records and coach newer agents
Add three wrong-gate examples to the team handbook before closing delayed-bag cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will settle the easy 'where is my bag' questions, and the rest will be missed connections and angry travellers. I would ask for the written paid rota before anyone promises our evening bonus is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hard-case skill may keep me on the desk, but a smaller late team could lose premium hours. David's stall has good and bad weeks, so eleven months saved would not make a permanent lower wage harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would learn the new AI routing checker by running fifteen closed wrong-city cases during paid time if my supervisor allows error logging. In the first year routine bag questions move, I would keep the paid evening disputes offered and ask for the written late rota; if the bonus or hours fall, I would compare posted local airline desks by full-week wages and hours before accepting a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the premium, excited to see whether the route checker catches a bad tag. A clever map cannot fill a shorter pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a routing failure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count a failure when the checker follows a flight number but misses that the bag was unloaded yesterday. Those are the cases where a person gets a confident wrong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change airport desks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave only for a signed paid offer whose weekly wages and hours still cover our bills after travel. The nearby airport may be hiring, but a longer journey can eat a small raise.

say: I would ask for the **written evening rota** before trusting a bonus promise.
I would tell colleagues **wrong-city cases** need paid human checking.
think: I could lose **premium hours** even if I retain hard claims.
I cannot rely on David's **variable stall income** to make lower weekly pay harmless.
do: Test **fifteen closed wrong-city cases** with new AI checker on paid time if error logging is approved.
Keep **paid evening disputes**; if hours fall, compare posted desks and move only on signed after-travel bill-covering weekly terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about premium pay while interested in a reliable checker.
S1.quote: A clever map cannot fill a shorter pay packet.
fieldNote: Her new **AI routing learning** uses closed cases, paid time and error-logging approval.
Any move needs a **signed offer** preserving full-week bill cover after a longer journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the desk that thinking AI by 2028 can trace and answer baggage claims before we can organise a new rota. Robots lifting and sorting bags arrive around 2031, but our screen work goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my paid calls could end quickly, including the evening premium. Eleven months saved and several nearby employers give us room to search, but they do not give David and me another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would request the written date of the paid claims change and total our rent, food and travel against the last four wage slips. If most hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid station customer work; I would accept only written full-week wages and hours covering bills after travel and keep any paid bag disputes until a real offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by how much of my own paid week could go. I can act, but a full savings account is not a new payroll department. Eleven months of savings do not create another baggage-claims wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about station work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a station customer post is actually paid to solve missed luggage, or just to point people at a screen. I would not spend the reserve on a course attached to no posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could David's stall cover the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: David's stall could be busy, but we would budget only the work he has booked and been paid for. Our daughter has her own rent; I will not call her a spare account.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** hits claims before 2031 baggage robots.
I would request a **written paid-change date** for the claims rota.
think: I expect **most paid calls** and my evening premium could end quickly.
I cannot count **eleven months saved** or unbooked stall work as a replacement wage.
do: Request the **written claims date** and compare four payslips with rent, food and travel.
After most **2028 hours end**, apply for posted paid station work; accept only written after-travel weekly wages and hours covering bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a major paid-week loss despite our reserve.
S2.quote: Eleven months of savings do not create another baggage-claims wage.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **posted paid station duties** from a screen-pointing or unposted course.
She budgets only **paid stall work**, while keeping offered claims until a real offer exists.

steps.text: Keep offered paid baggage disputes until a real role and request the written claims-change date
If most hours end after 2028, apply for posted paid station customer work
Accept only written full-week wages and hours covering bills after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to find out which parts of a luggage claim need a person, but not forever. Thinking AI can settle tags by 2031, with bag-handling robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still lead the awkward cases, though my evening bonus may shrink before the job ends. I have been sewing straps on our own cases for years, but I do not know whether anyone would pay me for that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would offer two safe strap repairs to travellers for an agreed small payment, only after checking that David's stall has room and the work will not delay his customers. I would keep my paid baggage shifts; if real customers pay and the repairs hold, I would continue the small service, but if my calls fall after 2031 I would still compare posted paid desk work by written weekly wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own calls, yet curious whether the sewing can earn a little without a lease or a loan. Two straps will tell me more than a grand business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repairs would you refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refuse a case with a cracked frame because a strap will not make it safe. I would start only with simple seams I already know and tell each customer what I can fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could two customers replace your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the repair money could never be our full income from two customers. David and I would count it only after it was paid, while checking actual statements before any decision to reduce our wages.

say: I would tell friends **2031 claim AI** comes before 2034 bag robots.
I would try **two paid strap repairs** without a lease or loan.
think: I may retain **awkward cases** while losing evening bonus hours.
I cannot assume a **repair income** before actual safe paying customers.
do: Offer **two simple strap repairs** for agreed pay only if David's stall has room.
Keep **paid baggage shifts**; continue repairs only if safe and paid, and compare posted desk wages if calls fall after 2031.
feel: I feel **anxious** about calls and curious about a small paid service.
S3.quote: Two straps will tell me more than a grand business plan.
fieldNote: Her **side-income trial** is limited to safe strap seams and two paying travellers.
She keeps **current paid shifts** and checks posted desk terms if calls later fall.

steps.text: Offer two paid strap repairs only if David has stall space and no customer delay
Keep paid baggage claims while testing whether safe repairs actually earn money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family ten years is enough to test a small repair service while a proper wage still comes in. Thinking AI reaches baggage decisions by 2036, and bag-moving robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer evening calls, but I cannot name what income replaces the bonus. Eleven months saved and two repaired straps are not a pension or a continuing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter David and I would gather actual income statements and count a full year of rent, bills and his stall receipts. I would keep paid bag claims and review the small repair earnings each quarter; after 2036 I would reduce paid shifts only if verified income covers our costs, otherwise keep the offered calls and any real repair customers. I would keep the repair work to safe seams at David’s stall, only if customers actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long-term desk change, steady about our savings today. I would rather have ten years of small honest numbers than one sweeping promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count repair income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put each repaired strap on the page only when its customer actually pays. A sewing box full of spare buckles is not an income statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can come by and laugh at the bright thread I use, but her rent is hers. I will not put her wage into our figures without a real offer from her.

say: I would use the **decade** to test repair income while earning wages.
I would explain **2036 claim AI** precedes 2039 bag robots.
think: I cannot name **replacement income** for evening bonuses at 68.
I see **eleven months saved** and two straps as buffers, not retirement pay.
do: Collect **wage and stall** statements against a year of bills.
Keep **paid baggage shifts** and count paid repairs quarterly; reduce shifts only if verified income covers costs.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later work, with savings and paid shifts today.
S4.quote: A sewing box full of spare buckles is not an income statement.
fieldNote: She counts **paid repair earnings** only when customers pay, while continuing safe simple seams.

steps.text: Keep offered paid baggage claims while checking actual repair receipts each quarter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because most of the paid baggage week could go before a station post opens. Written hours and a real local job whose full-week pay covers rent after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who phones the traveller when the bag arrives in the wrong city after a confident automated answer. Someone still has to say where the bag actually is.

headlineQuote: Someone still has to say where the bag actually is.
portrait: A **58-year-old** senior baggage-claims agent with a two-year college diploma and strong difficult-case skill.
She uses **AI search daily** while checking dated baggage tags and flight records.
Her **higher evening pay**, eleven-month reserve and many nearby desks give her search room.
She tests **small safe strap repairs** as side income while keeping wages and verifying later-life income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most paid baggage hours before another suitable station post opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** and a real local role with after-travel full-week bill cover would help.
